title: HTTP by hand over TCP
summary: The layers of the networking stack, what an HTTP request and response look like on the wire, TcpStream and TcpListener with a local server, ports and sockets, converting host names to addresses with ToSocketAddrs, UDP datagrams, timeouts, and where reqwest fits in.

sections: RiA 8.2 Generating an HTTP GET request with reqwest
RiA 8.4.1 What is a port number?
RiA 8.4.2 Converting a hostname to an IP address

blocks.md:
Networking is built in **layers**. Each layer uses the one below and knows nothing about the one above:

- **Application**: HTTP, DNS, SMTP. What programs say to each other.
- **Security**: TLS, which encrypts HTTP into HTTPS.
- **Transport**: TCP (a reliable, ordered byte stream) or UDP (independent datagrams, no guarantees).
- **Network**: IP, which routes packets between addresses.
- **Link**: Ethernet or Wi-Fi, which moves frames between neighbouring machines identified by MAC addresses.

*Rust in Action* works down the stack. It starts with HTTP, because almost every program talks it.

blocks.title: An HTTP request is text
blocks.md:
HTTP/1.x messages are lines of text separated by **`\r\n`** (carriage return, line feed). A request has a **request line** (method, path, version), **headers**, an empty line, and an optional body. The response has a **status line** (`HTTP/1.1 200 OK`), headers, an empty line and the body:

```text
GET /index.html HTTP/1.1\r\n
Host: www.rustinaction.com\r\n
\r\n
```

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK\r\n
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8\r\n
Content-Length: 13\r\n
\r\n
Hello, world!
```

The `Host` header matters because one IP address can serve many websites. `Content-Length` tells the client where the body ends.

blocks.title: TCP in the standard library
blocks.md: `std::net::TcpStream::connect(addr)` opens a TCP connection; the stream implements `Read` and `Write`, so everything from chapter 22 applies. *Rust in Action* connects to `www.rustinaction.com:80` and writes the request with `write_all`. The course console has no internet access, so the example below starts its own tiny server with **`TcpListener`** on the loopback address `127.0.0.1`, port `0` (meaning "pick any free port"), in a second thread, and then talks to it like a browser would.

blocks.output:
HTTP/1.0 200 OK
Content-Length: 20

you asked for /hello
blocks.explain: HTTP/1.0 closes the connection after the response, so `read_to_string` ends when the server's stream is dropped. Real HTTP/1.1 keeps connections alive and needs `Content-Length` to know when to stop reading. `\r\n` is replaced only to print the response neatly.

steps.title: bind and listen
steps.md: `TcpListener::bind` asks the operating system for a **socket** on an address and port and starts accepting connections.

steps.title: The three-way handshake
steps.md: `TcpStream::connect` sends SYN, the server's kernel replies SYN-ACK, the client sends ACK. Only then does `accept` return a stream on the server side.

steps.title: Bytes, not messages
steps.md: TCP delivers a **stream** of bytes, in order, retransmitting lost packets. It has no idea where one HTTP message ends: that is HTTP's job (the blank line, `Content-Length`).

steps.title: Closing
steps.md: Dropping a stream closes it (FIN). The reader on the other side sees end of file: `read` returns 0.

blocks.title: Ports and addresses
blocks.md:
A **port** is just a `u16` that lets one IP address host many services: 80 for HTTP, 443 for HTTPS, 22 for SSH, 53 for DNS. Ports below 1024 usually need administrator rights. An IP address plus a port is a **socket address**, `SocketAddr` in Rust, either `SocketAddrV4` (`127.0.0.1:8080`) or `SocketAddrV6` (`[::1]:8080`).

TCP knows nothing about names like `www.rustinaction.com`. **DNS** turns names into IP addresses. *Rust in Action* writes a DNS resolver with a crate; the standard library offers **`ToSocketAddrs`**, which asks the operating system's resolver and is what `connect("host:port")` uses internally:

blocks.output:
ip 192.168.1.20 port 8080 v4? true
127.0.0.1 loopback? true
true
true
[127.0.0.1:80]

blocks.title: UDP
blocks.md: **UDP** sends individual **datagrams**. There is no connection, no ordering and no retransmission: a datagram arrives whole or not at all. That makes it fast and simple, which is why DNS and NTP (lesson 3) use it. `UdpSocket::bind` gets a socket; `send_to` and `recv_from` move one datagram at a time.

blocks.explain: A read timeout matters with UDP: if the reply datagram is lost, `recv_from` would otherwise wait forever. It returns an error of kind `WouldBlock` or `TimedOut` when the time runs out.

blocks.title: reqwest
blocks.md: For real HTTP clients, *Rust in Action* starts with the **reqwest** crate: `reqwest::blocking::get(url)?.text()?` handles DNS, TLS, redirects, keep-alive and chunked bodies. Use it (or `ureq`) in practice. It needs crates.io, so this course shows the protocol by hand instead.

blocks.title: An echo server
blocks.md: Complete the server thread: accept one connection, then read lines with a `BufReader` and write each one back in upper case, until the client closes. The client sends three lines and then shuts down its writing half with `shutdown(Shutdown::Write)` so the server sees end of file.
hints: `stream.try_clone()?` gives a second handle to the same connection: read from one, write to the other.

blocks.title: A minimal HTTP client and parser
blocks.goal: Build and parse HTTP/1.x messages, and run a request against a real TCP server on the loopback interface.
blocks.behavior:
- `pub fn build_request(method: &str, host: &str, path: &str, body: &str) -> String`: request line `METHOD PATH HTTP/1.1`, headers `Host`, `Connection: close` and, if the body is not empty, `Content-Length`; every line ends with `\r\n`, then a blank line, then the body.
- `pub struct Response { pub status: u16, pub reason: String, pub headers: Vec<(String, String)>, pub body: String }` with `pub fn header(&self, name: &str) -> Option<&str>` (case-insensitive).
- `pub fn parse_response(raw: &str) -> Result<Response, String>`: split head and body at the first `\r\n\r\n`; parse the status line (`HTTP/1.x CODE REASON`, reason may contain spaces); headers are `Name: value` (trim the value); if `Content-Length` is present, the body is exactly that many bytes. Errors (as `Err(String)`) for a missing blank line, a bad status line or a malformed header.
- `pub fn fetch(addr: SocketAddr, path: &str) -> std::io::Result<Response>`: connect, send a GET, read everything, parse (map a parse error to `io::ErrorKind::InvalidData`).
hints: Status line: `let mut parts = line.splitn(3, ' ');` gives version, code and the rest.
blocks.solution_explain: `split_once` and `splitn(3, ' ')` do most of the parsing; the reason phrase keeps its spaces because it is the third, unsplit part. `Connection: close` makes the server close after responding, which is why `read_to_string` in `fetch` terminates.

points: Networks are layered: application (HTTP), security (TLS), transport (TCP/UDP), network (IP), link (Ethernet).
HTTP/1.x is text: a request line, headers, a blank line and an optional body, with \r\n line endings.
TcpStream and TcpListener give byte streams that implement Read and Write.
A socket address is an IP and a port; ToSocketAddrs resolves names through the OS.
UdpSocket sends datagrams without connections; set timeouts because packets can be lost.

terms.def: An agreed set of message formats and rules for two programs to communicate.
Transmission Control Protocol: a reliable, ordered byte stream between two sockets.
User Datagram Protocol: independent datagrams with no delivery guarantees.
A 16-bit number identifying a service on a host.
An IP address combined with a port.
The Domain Name System, which maps names like example.com to IP addresses.
The address 127.0.0.1 (or ::1) that always refers to the local machine.
